criteria.name: Introduction — Identifies ethical issues and broad links to engineering design; discusses the context of ethical issues in engineering organisations; identifies relevant stakeholders when considering the ethical issues.
criteria.reasoning: Introduction identifies the core ethical dilemma, links it to engineering design and organisational competition, and explicitly lists stakeholders. Significance of public harm and professional responsibility is noted, so both context and stakeholder interest are demonstrated.

evidence.quote: The relevant stakeholders in this scenario include Rachel, Rachel’s company, the chip contract company, the government health department

criteria.name: Balanced Discussion — Discusses objective arguments for and against decisions on the ethical issues; draws a conclusion on how stakeholders should make decisions about the issues.
criteria.reasoning: Balanced for-and-against arguments are presented with a clear conclusion. Depth is moderate: some claims are speculative, and decision recommendations focus mainly on Rachel and her company rather than several distinct stakeholders.

criteria.name: Compelling Argument that supports conclusion — The report forms a compelling argument that justifies the conclusion; the body follows a logical structure, with linked paragraphs and content ordered to support the argument; arguments demonstrate a systematic understanding of the ethical issues for all stakeholders.
criteria.reasoning: The report has a logical structure and the conclusion follows from the arguments. It is compelling overall, but does not systematically analyse every stakeholder, especially the chip contractor, so it falls short of Excellent.

evidence.quote: As seen by the points raised in the discussion, it is clear that Rachel faces a difficult decision.

criteria.name: Research and Evidence — Arguments are substantiated with adequate references and qualitative/quantitative evidence; research demonstrates a balanced, in-depth understanding of the topic.
criteria.reasoning: Arguments are supported by relevant external cases and the Engineers Australia code. Qualitative evidence is adequate, but quantitative evidence is absent and references are limited, so it is not Excellent.

criteria.name: Report Structure, Format and Language — The report includes appropriate sections serving their functions (abstract, introduction, body, and conclusion); maps, figures, tables, and visual elements are correctly used to support discussion; writing is grammatically correct, fluent, concise, easy to read and understand, and uses appropriate word choice; references are well-structured and appropriate, supporting the report’s motivations.
criteria.reasoning: Required sections are present and writing is mostly readable, but there are language slips, no figures or tables, and references are incomplete or malformed. Visual elements are absent, limiting this criterion.

technical_issues.issue: Apple/CNBC example supports consumer release strategy, not an ethical argument or evidence for shipping defective servers.
EACE clause 2.3b concerns competence and qualifications, not insufficient QA time or resources; the citation is misapplied.
The competitor-will-ship argument is speculative and unsupported by evidence.
No explicit conditions are given for when a product with known defects may be shipped; the recommendation is a blanket refusal.
The six-month release cycle and a six-month QA window are conflated.
Reference [3] lacks a URL; [1] has a malformed URL; [4] has incorrect author formatting; no quantitative evidence is provided.

overall: A well-structured, balanced report with a clear recommendation and relevant cases, but evidence is thin, some arguments are speculative, EACE clause use is imprecise, references are incomplete, and no visual elements are used. Most scenario requirements are met; R2, R3 and R6 only partially.

feedback.summary: Your report is well structured and balanced, with a clear recommendation and relevant cases (HSSIB, Volkswagen). You identify ethical issues and stakeholders well. However, evidence is thin, some arguments are speculative, EACE clause 2.3b is misapplied, references are incomplete, and no visual elements are used. Most scenario requirements are met; R2, R3 and R6 only partially.
next_steps: Add quantitative evidence (e.g., defect rates, recall costs, injury statistics) and correct all references: provide a URL for [3], fix the malformed URL in [1], and correct the author formatting in [4].

Deepen stakeholder analysis: give decision-making recommendations for the chip contractor, health department, and end-users, and replace speculative claims (e.g., competitor-will-ship) with supported reasoning.
Include at least one visual element (stakeholder map or decision flowchart) and proofread for language slips (e.g., 'DICUSSION') to raise C5.

criteria.C1: You clearly identify ethical issues, link them to engineering design and organisational competition, and list stakeholders in the Introduction. This meets Excellent. To sustain this level, carry the stakeholder analysis through the body so each group’s interests are revisited in the discussion.
criteria.C2: You present balanced for-and-against arguments and a clear conclusion, but depth is moderate and recommendations focus mainly on Rachel and her company. To reach Excellent, deepen the arguments and make decision-making recommendations for several distinct stakeholders (e.g., chip contractor, health department, end-users). Avoid unsupported claims like the competitor-will-ship argument.
criteria.C3: Your report has a logical structure and the conclusion follows from the arguments, but it does not systematically analyse every stakeholder, especially the chip contractor. To reach Excellent, ensure each section builds a compelling case and systematically addresses the ethical issues for all stakeholders, not just Rachel and her company.
criteria.C4: You use relevant external cases (HSSIB, Volkswagen) and the Engineers Australia code, but quantitative evidence is absent and references are limited. To reach Excellent, add quantitative data (e.g., defect rates, recall costs) and strengthen references (complete URLs, correct formatting). Ensure evidence directly supports ethical arguments—the Apple/CNBC example supports consumer release strategy, not shipping defective servers.
criteria.C5: Required sections are present and writing is mostly readable, but there are language slips (e.g., 'DICUSSION'), no figures or tables, and references are incomplete or malformed ([3] lacks URL, [1] malformed URL, [4] incorrect author formatting). To reach Good, proofread for language errors, add at least one visual element (e.g., stakeholder map or decision flowchart), and correct reference formatting.
